title: Compliance Programs and Audit Readiness

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the elements of an effective compliance program.
- Explain audit readiness and the practices that keep a medical office prepared for payer audits.
- Recognize the role of accurate documentation in supporting billed services and medical necessity.
- Describe internal auditing and monitoring activities and their corrective purpose.
- Apply correct procedures for responding to audits and correcting errors without altering records.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A compliance program is like the rules and safety checks on a school bus: they exist to help everyone follow the rules and catch mistakes before anyone gets hurt.

### Question 2

Written policies are like the instruction book for a board game: everyone can read the rules so they all play fairly the same way.

### Question 3

Think of the seven elements like the seven pieces of a complete tool kit; each one does a different job, and together they keep the office on track.

### Question 4

Compliance is like a class keeping its classroom clean: the teacher leads and someone coordinates, but every student has to pick up their own mess.

### Question 5

A code of conduct is like a team's list of promises about how everyone will treat each other and do the right thing.

### Question 6

The compliance officer is like the team captain whose job is to watch the whole game and help everyone follow the rules.

### Question 7

A confidential hotline is like a suggestion box with a lock: people can point out a problem honestly without worrying about being punished for speaking up.

### Question 8

Compliance training is like practicing a sport: you do not learn it once and stop; you keep practicing so everyone stays sharp.

### Question 9

Fair discipline is like the rules on a playground: the same rules apply to everyone, and breaking them has a clear, fair consequence.

### Question 10

Responding to a problem is like fixing a leaky pipe: you find the leak, repair it, and then check why it leaked so it does not happen again.

### Question 11

Internal auditing is like checking your own homework before turning it in: you catch mistakes while you still have time to fix them.

### Question 12

The policies manual is like the official rulebook: when you are unsure, you check the book rather than asking someone to guess.

### Question 13

If you see someone breaking the rules, you tell a trusted adult quietly instead of shouting about it in the hallway or trying to fix it yourself.

### Question 14

Tone at the top is like parents wearing seatbelts: when the people in charge follow the rules, everyone else is more likely to follow them too.

### Question 15

Good training is like brushing your teeth: it is not a one-time thing; you do it regularly to stay healthy.

### Question 16

A compliance program without a leader or written rules is like a sports team with no coach and no playbook: the team is far more likely to make mistakes.

### Question 17

Good rules are like the posted rules at a swimming pool: they are written clearly, kept up to date, and hung where everyone can read them.

### Question 18

The seven elements are like the seven important jobs on a team; written rules, practice, and checking your own work are three of those jobs.

### Question 19

The compliance committee is like a group of assistant coaches who help the head coach keep everyone following the rules.

### Question 20

Even a small team needs a designated captain; if no one is officially in charge, small problems can grow because no one is watching the whole game.

### Question 21

When a test shows a wrong answer, you do not just erase it; you figure out why you got it wrong and practice so you do not repeat the mistake.

### Question 22

A compliance program is like the railings on a staircase: they do not stop every possible fall, but they make falls much less likely.

### Question 23

Audit readiness is like keeping your room tidy so that when someone asks for something, you can find it right away instead of searching in a panic.

### Question 24

Documentation is like the receipt for a purchase: if you are asked whether you really bought something, the receipt is your proof.

### Question 25

When a teacher asks for your homework, you turn it in on time with the actual work, not an empty page.

### Question 26

Keeping orders and permissions on file is like saving a permission slip for a field trip: if asked, you can show you were allowed to go.

### Question 27

Filing records right away is like putting your toys back where they belong so you can find them later without a big hunt.

### Question 28

An audit-ready office is like a well-organized backpack: everything is in place and easy to pull out when the teacher asks.

### Question 29

Tracking denials is like noticing you keep losing points on the same type of test question, then studying that part so you stop losing points.

### Question 30

Being ready is like keeping your desk clean all year, not just shoving everything into a drawer when the teacher walks by.

### Question 31

If some pages of your report are smudged and unsigned, the teacher may not accept them; you fix the habit going forward, not fake the work later.

### Question 32

If you do not know an answer, it is smarter to say you will check with someone who does than to make something up.

### Question 33

For an E/M audit, the clinical note is like the recipe for a dish: it shows exactly what went into the service being billed.

### Question 34

A probe review is like a pop quiz on a few problems; you do your best honest work on those and turn it in on time.

### Question 35

Keeping a map of where things are is like labeling the boxes in your attic so you can find the winter coats without unpacking everything.

### Question 36

Writing things down right away is like jotting a note while the idea is fresh, instead of trying to remember it a week later.

### Question 37

If many homework papers lack a signature line, the fix is a routine for getting them signed, not pretending the signature exists.

### Question 38

Checking eligibility is like checking you have enough money before buying lunch, so you are not surprised when the bill comes.

### Question 39

If you charge for a service you cannot show you performed, it is like charging for a product with no receipt or record of the work.

### Question 40

You build readiness the way you build fitness: a little every day, not by trying to run a marathon the night before.

### Question 41

An internal audit is like grading your own quiz before the teacher sees it, so you can fix mistakes first.

### Question 42

The point of checking your own work is to catch and fix mistakes early, not to get anyone in trouble.

### Question 43

Prospective means looking forward, like checking your answers before you hand in the paper.

### Question 44

Retrospective means looking backward, like reviewing a game recording afterward to see what you could have done better.

### Question 45

Prospective is checking your homework before turning it in; retrospective is reviewing it after it has been graded.

### Question 46

Checking a random few papers every month is like spot-checking your work regularly so small mistakes do not pile up.

### Question 47

A baseline audit is like taking a photo on day one of a fitness plan, so later you can see how much you improved.

### Question 48

A fair sample is like tasting soup after stirring it, not just scooping from one corner of the pot.

### Question 49

A coding and documentation review is like checking that the description on the menu matches what is actually on the plate.

### Question 50

If you find you have been scoring a test too high by mistake, you fix the scoring and learn the right way, not change the answers to keep the high score.

### Question 51

The best result of checking your work is knowing exactly what to study next, not finding someone to blame.

### Question 52

You know a fix worked only when you check again later and the mistake is really gone, like re-testing after studying.

### Question 53

You would want someone who knows the rules to check the work, like a coach with experience, not someone who has never seen the game.

### Question 54

Monitoring is like glancing at the road while you drive; auditing is like taking the car in for a full inspection.

### Question 55

If a typo keeps appearing in many papers, you fix the typo, teach everyone the right spelling, and update the template, not keep making the mistake.

### Question 56

When cleaning a messy room, you start with the corner that matters most, not try to clean everything in one minute.

### Question 57

If you return a library book but there is no record, the library cannot tell it was returned; a record is the proof.

### Question 58

Documentation is like the proof of work: before anyone pays for a job, they want to see that the work was really done.

### Question 59

Medically necessary is like a doctor's order that is actually needed to help you get better, not just something extra you asked for.

### Question 60

A diagnosis is supported when the note shows the clues that match it, like a label that matches what you actually see in the picture.

### Question 61

If a piece of homework is missing, you tell the teacher so it can be completed properly, not write it yourself and sign someone else's name.

### Question 62

Each billed code needs its own matching description, like each item on a receipt matching something actually purchased.

### Question 63

Choose the label that matches the work actually done, like picking the shirt size that really fits rather than the biggest one on the rack.

### Question 64

Undercoding is like undercharging for a job by describing it as smaller than it really was.

### Question 65

Copying the same sentence into every book report means none of them really describe the book you read.

### Question 66

A signature and date are like signing a letter: they show who wrote it and when, so everyone knows it is real.

### Question 67

If a receipt says you bought a fancy meal but the note shows only a snack, the person checking will lower the charge to match what is written.

### Question 68

You should never write down things that did not happen just to make a paper look better; that is like changing answers after the test is over.

### Question 69

Supporting a procedure is like showing your work on a math problem: the steps, the reason, and the answer all need to be there.

### Question 70

Before sending a bill, check the receipt matches what you actually did, like proofreading before you hit send.

### Question 71

Linkage is like showing that the reason for a repair matches the work done, so the bill makes sense.

### Question 72

If a note is hard to read, ask the person who wrote it instead of guessing what it says.

### Question 73

When you get an important letter, you note the due date and hand it to the right person, not ignore it or scribble on it.

### Question 74

You show your real work exactly as it is, not a rewritten version, because changing it would not be honest.

### Question 75

One designated person is in charge of answering the important letter, like one student chosen to speak for the whole group.

### Question 76

When homework is due in 30 days, you start early and make sure it is ready, not wait until the last minute.

### Question 77

If a cashier gives you too much change, the honest thing is to return the extra, not keep it or hide it.

### Question 78

If you find a mistake in an official paper, you tell the person in charge how to fix it properly, not erase or scribble over it.

### Question 79

An appeal is like asking a teacher to re-grade a test because you think a mistake was made, using the proper request form.

### Question 80

If someone asks for a paper you never wrote, you say so honestly rather than making one up.

### Question 81

A corrective action plan is like a to-do list for fixing a problem so it does not happen again.

### Question 82

When a letter seems important and complicated, you ask the person in charge how to handle it before sending anything.

### Question 83

When a bill says you owe money, you check whether it is correct and then pay or dispute it by the due date, not ignore it.

### Question 84

After a test, you look at the questions you missed and study those, so the next test goes better.

### Question 85

These programs are like referees who review the game afterward to check that the score was fair and correct.
